hints: Look carefully at what holds each solid together, both within the particles and between the particles in the solid.
Picture solid iodine as $\text{I}_2$ molecules packed together, so ask what holds the two I atoms together and what holds one molecule to the next.
Compare that to the other three, which are giant lattices with only one repeating bond type throughout, to spot the one with two different interactions.
walkthrough:
**Separate Within From Between**

Think like a detective. For a molecular solid you need two answers: what bonds atoms together inside the molecule, and what attracts molecules to each other in the solid.

Strong bond inside + weak force between = two types.

**Check Iodine**

Iodine is $\text{I}_2$ molecules in a lattice. Inside each molecule the two iodine atoms share electrons.

$$\text{I} - \text{I} : \text{ covalent bond inside molecule }$$
Between the $\text{I}_2$ molecules there are only weak London dispersion forces (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces) holding the solid together.

**Check The Giant Structures**

Silicon dioxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, is giant covalent with only $\text{Si}-\text{O}$ covalent bonds throughout. Sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$, is giant ionic with only ionic attraction between $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$. Zinc, $\text{Zn}$, is giant metallic with only metallic bonding.

Only iodine needs two different descriptions, so it is the answer.

options.A: Correct. Solid iodine contains covalent bonding within each $\text{I}_2$ molecule and London dispersion forces between the $\text{I}_2$ molecules. That is more than one type of bonding or interaction.
options.B: Not correct. Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent lattice with only one bond type, covalent $\text{Si}-\text{O}$ bonds in a continuous network. Students sometimes confuse the different atoms with different bond types, but all the bonds are covalent.
options.C: Not correct. Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice with only ionic bonding between $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions. There is no covalent or metallic bonding present.
options.D: Not correct. Zinc is a metal with only metallic bonding, positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. There is no second bond type inside the pure metal.
